title: Epic: one versioned recommendation algorithm
body: ## Problem
Nothing names the algorithm that makes a recommendation. A ranked weakness depends on about thirty
constants, protocols, prompt files and model ids across eight crates and the web app:
`ANALYSIS_PROTOCOL` (`sf19-n300k-v1`), `ENRICHMENT_PROTOCOL` (`enr-v1`), `DETECTOR_VERSION`
(`tl-v1`), `PLAYER_GAME_METRICS_VERSION` (3), `RANK_MIN_EXCESS_PER_GAME` (0.02), the trainer's
intervals, the prompt sets. A change to any of them shows only in the diff, and no stored row says
which rules produced it. Determinism is partly an accident: the engine pool sends neither
`Threads` nor `Hash` (`backend/crates/engine/src/pool.rs`), so searches are reproducible because
Stockfish's defaults are 1 and 16 MB, and only `server/stats` is checked for `Math.random`.
## Who it's for
Every player, who should be able to see which rules produced a recommendation; contributors, who
change those rules; and the evaluation lab (v0.3), which compares algorithm versions.
## Goals
1. **A manifest.** `algorithm/manifest.json` names every component of the facts, profile and
recommendation layers and the language layer's prompt sets and models, generated from the code.
2. **An id and a policy.** `algo-<major>.<minor>.<patch>+<hash12>`: major when facts, profile or
recommendation can change, minor when only the language layer changes, patch when a replay sees
nothing. `algorithm/CHANGELOG.md` has one entry per version.
3. **A CI guard.** A component change without a version bump and a changelog entry fails.
4. **Stamping.** `algorithm_id` on every row a recommendation comes from.
5. **A replay suite.** The same games and the same id give byte-identical facts, profile rows and
CoachingInput, on two machines.
6. **Run records and history** for the benchmark (the first two pieces of the evaluation lab), so
v0.3 can compare versions.
## Non-goals
- A deterministic language model. The check on which recommendation a text names is deterministic;
the wording is not and need not be.
- Re-analysing stored games when the version changes.
## Evidence
- The Tier 1 benchmark already proves part of the contract: `backend/crates/bench/tests/pipeline.rs`
generates a game twice, and score (e) builds the CoachingInput twice (`docs/benchmark.md`).
- ADR 0101 changed the ranking and three prompt versions in one branch; nothing outside the diff
recorded that reports written before and after use different rules.
- The bootstrap became seeded on 2026-11-23 after the same games gave different ranges.
## Proposed design
The spec (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-24-factual-deterministic-evaluation-design.md`), sections 2 to 4 and 9:
- a new `backend/crates/algo` crate that rebuilds the manifest from the constants it imports and
digests the files that hold unnamed constants (`profile-core/src/constants.rs`, `stats/`,
`weakness/detectors.rs`);
- the id in `common::algorithm` (`include_str!` of the manifest), so writers need no new
dependency;
- a migration with `algorithm_versions (id, manifest)` and `algorithm_id` on ten tables;
- `Threads 1` and `Hash 16` sent explicitly, and an audit test of the UCI lines;
- a ban on unseeded randomness and the wall clock in the maths modules, Rust and TS;
- golden snapshots of a canonical dump, compared on every pull request that touches the pipeline.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every sub-issue below is done.
- [ ] Changing one threshold (for example `RANK_MIN_EXCESS_PER_GAME`) on a branch fails CI until the
version is bumped, the goldens regenerated and a changelog entry added.
- [ ] The replay suite gives byte-identical dumps twice in a row, locally and on the CI runner.
- [ ] A new report, chat answer, weekly review, focus and drill item each carry the current
`algorithm_id`, and `algorithm_versions` holds its manifest.
- [ ] Adding an unseeded `Math.random` to `apps/web/src/server/train/model.ts` fails the test.
## Test plan
- Rust: the manifest test, the UCI audit, the replay suite and a DB test per stamped writer.
- TS: the manifest's TS fields, the randomness and clock ban, the web writers' stamp.
- CI: `scripts/algorithm/check.mjs` against a fixture pair of manifests (bumped, not bumped,
changelog missing).
## ADR
ADR 0104 (accepted). A new ADR only if the version policy changes.
## Risks and open questions
- Digesting whole files turns a comment edit into a patch bump. The patch policy (identical goldens)
keeps that cheap; if it proves noisy, digest only the items between markers.
- The `algo` crate depends on `ai`, `profile` and `engine`; it must stay a leaf. Writers read the
id from `common`.
- `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock` changes go through the coordinator (CLAUDE.md); the new crate uses
workspace path dependencies only.
## Pointers
- `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-24-factual-deterministic-evaluation-design.md`
- `backend/crates/engine/src/{types,pool,uci}.rs`, `backend/crates/enrich/src/protocol.rs`
- `backend/crates/profile-core/src/{types,constants}.rs`, `stats/priority.rs`, `timeline/states.rs`
- `backend/crates/ai/src/prompts.rs`, `backend/crates/ai/src/client/model.rs`
- `apps/web/src/server/train/model.ts`, `apps/web/src/server/focus/goal.ts`

title: Name the algorithm: an algo crate and algorithm/manifest.json
body: ## Problem
There is no single place that says which rules produce a recommendation, so no row, report or
benchmark can say which version it came from.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A new workspace crate `backend/crates/algo` (path dependencies only; the coordinator edits
`Cargo.toml`) builds the manifest of the spec's section 3 from the real constants:
`engine::ANALYSIS_PROTOCOL`, `ENGINE_NODES`, `enrich::protocol::*`, `DETECTOR_VERSION`,
`PLAYER_GAME_METRICS_VERSION`, `INPUT_VERSION`, `WEEKLY_INPUT_VERSION`,
`prompt_set_hash` of every `*_PROMPT_SET`, `AiModel::ALL`, `ANTHROPIC_VERSION`.
- [ ] New constants: `RANKING_VERSION = "rank-v1"` in `profile-core/src/stats/priority.rs`,
`TRAINER_VERSION = "trainer-v1"` in `apps/web/src/server/train/model.ts` and
`FOCUS_VERSION = "focus-v1"` in `apps/web/src/server/focus/goal.ts`.
- [ ] `source_digest` fields: sha256 of each listed file with CRLF normalised to LF.
- [ ] The Stockfish asset and sha256 are read from `backend/Dockerfile`'s `ARG` lines, the Syzygy
digest from `backend/crates/lichess-db/data/syzygy-345.sha256`, Maia from
`services/maia/pyproject.toml`.
- [ ] `algorithm_id` is `algo-<version>+<first 12 hex of sha256(canonical JSON)>`; canonical JSON has
sorted keys and no whitespace, with a unit test pinning one known id.
- [ ] `cargo run -p cli -- algo manifest --write` writes `algorithm/manifest.json`;
`algo manifest` alone prints it.
- [ ] `common::algorithm::id()` and `manifest()` read the committed file with `include_str!`;
`backend/Dockerfile.dockerignore` gains `!algorithm/` and both build stages copy it.
- [ ] `algorithm/CHANGELOG.md` starts with the first version, `algo-1.0.0`, and today's Tier 1
scorecard as its baseline.
## Pointers
- Spec section 3; ADR 0104 decisions 2 and 3.
- `backend/crates/common` for the id, `backend/crates/cli` for the command.

title: Fail CI on an algorithm change without a version bump and a changelog entry
body: ## Problem
A manifest nobody checks drifts. The point is that a change to a threshold cannot merge silently.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A test in `backend/crates/algo` rebuilds the manifest and fails with a readable diff when the
committed `algorithm/manifest.json` differs.
- [ ] A web test (`apps/web/test/algorithm.test.ts`) checks the manifest's TS fields against
`TRAINER_VERSION`, `FOCUS_VERSION`, `PHASE_METRICS_VERSION` and the digests of the TS files.
- [ ] `scripts/algorithm/check.mjs` (Node, no dependencies) compares the manifest with the merge
base's: a changed component needs a version bump that fits the policy (major for layers 1 to
3, minor for the language layer only, patch only when the replay goldens are unchanged) and
an `algorithm/CHANGELOG.md` entry headed with the new id.
- [ ] Wired into the `ts` job of `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; its own tests run with
`node scripts/algorithm/test-check.mjs` on fixture manifests.
- [ ] Each changelog entry has: what changed, why, the ADR, and the benchmark delta (from
`cli bench compare` once it exists, else the scorecard before and after).
## Pointers
- Spec section 3 (the CI guard); `scripts/github/test-settings.mjs` for the dependency-free test style.

title: Stamp algorithm_id on every row a recommendation comes from
body: ## Problem
A stored report, focus or estimate cannot say which rules produced it, so an old report cannot be
told apart from a new one after a ranking change.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A migration in `db/migrations/` adds `algorithm_versions (id text PRIMARY KEY, manifest jsonb
NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())`.
- [ ] A nullable `algorithm_id text REFERENCES algorithm_versions (id)` on `coaching_inputs`,
`report_runs`, `weekly_reviews`, `coach_messages`, `focuses`, `drill_items`,
`kpi_snapshot`, `weakness_estimates`, `weakness_state_history` and `game_metrics`.
`position_evals` keeps its (`fen_key`, `protocol`) key and gets no column.
- [ ] The worker inserts its manifest at start-up (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`).
- [ ] Every Rust writer fills the column from `common::algorithm::id()`; the web writers of
`focuses` and `drill_items` from the same manifest file. A DB test per writer.
- [ ] The Drizzle schema in `apps/web` matches the migration (the schema check passes).
- [ ] Existing rows stay `NULL` ("before versioning"); nothing is backfilled.
## Pointers
- Spec section 4; ADR 0086 (the snapshot writer, `profile::coaching::snapshot`), ADR 0090
(`drill_items`), ADR 0091 (`focuses`).

title: Send Threads and Hash explicitly, and test the UCI lines the engine receives
body: ## Problem
The pool starts engines with `threads: None` (`backend/crates/engine/src/pool.rs`) and the worker
with `hash_mb: None` (`backend/crates/worker/src/start.rs`). Searches are reproducible only because
Stockfish's defaults are 1 thread and 16 MB. A different Stockfish build with other defaults would
change every evaluation without a line of our code changing.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `StartOptions` from the pool always sends `setoption name Threads value 1` and
`setoption name Hash value 16`; the worker's `PoolOptions` sets `hash_mb: Some(16)`.
- [ ] A test in `backend/crates/engine/tests/` drives a fake UCI engine (a small script that logs its
stdin) through the pool and asserts: Threads 1, Hash 16, `ucinewgame` before every
`position`, and `go nodes <n>` with the requested count, never `go movetime`.
- [ ] The manifest's `facts.engine_options` names both values.
## Pointers
- `UciEngine::handshake` and `UciEngine::analyse` in `backend/crates/engine/src/uci.rs`.
- Spec section 2 (the engine settings table).

title: Ban unseeded randomness and the wall clock in the maths modules
body: ## Problem
Only `apps/web/src/server/stats` is checked for `Math.random`
(`apps/web/test/stats/bootstrap.test.ts`). The trainer, the focus and the profile maths are not, and
the Rust side has no check at all.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The TS test covers `server/stats`, `server/train/model.ts`, `server/focus/goal.ts`,
`server/overview` and `server/profile`, and bans `Math.random`, `Date.now()` and
`new Date()` with no argument.
- [ ] A Rust test bans `rand::`, `thread_rng`, `SystemTime::now` and `OffsetDateTime::now_utc` in
the `src/` of `profile-core`, `enrich` and `coaching-input`, and in the maths modules of
`profile`.
- [ ] An allow-list names each legitimate use with a reason, and a planted call fails the test.
## Pointers
- `profile_core::stats::rng` (mulberry32), `mulberry32` and `dataSeed` in
`apps/web/src/server/stats/bootstrap.ts`. Spec section 2 (randomness and the clock).

title: A replay suite: the same games give byte-identical facts, profile and recommendations
body: ## Problem
Determinism is claimed and tested only in slices (the bench generator, the CoachingInput built twice).
Nothing runs the whole pipeline twice on real games and compares what it stored.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A replay test runs import, analysis, enrichment and build-profile twice, in two throwaway
databases, on `backend/fixtures/pgn/*.pgn`, `backend/fixtures/lichess-db/sample.pgn`,
`backend/fixtures/lichess-games.ndjson` and `backend/fixtures/chesscom-month.json`.
- [ ] A canonical dump of the tables in spec section 2: natural-key order, wall-clock columns and row
ids removed, floats as shortest round-trip decimals, the CoachingInput as canonical JSON.
- [ ] The two dumps are byte-identical, and equal to golden files in
`backend/crates/algo/tests/golden/`. A diff prints the first differing table and row.
- [ ] `REPLAY_UPDATE=1` regenerates the goldens; the CI guard accepts new goldens only with a major
version bump.
- [ ] Runs on the CI runner and locally with the same goldens (the two-machine check), at a node count
small enough for CI, recorded in the golden header.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/bench/src/harness.rs` (in-process pipeline), `backend/crates/testkit`.
- Spec section 2 (what must be byte-identical, how it is tested).

title: Check that the recommendation a text names is the computed one
body: ## Problem
The validator drops uncited facts (ADRs 0093, 0102), but nothing checks that the coach's text leads
with the recommendation the CoachingInput and the plan context computed. A report could cite a real
weakness and still recommend the wrong one first.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A deterministic check, from the citation tokens only: the report's weaknesses section and
climb plan lead with the CoachingInput's top-ranked weakness; a chat answer that suggests a drill
or a focus names the plan context's (ADR 0094); the weekly review's focus is the running focus.
- [ ] A mismatch is recorded on the stored item (`report_sections.dropped` reason
`recommendation_mismatch`, `coach_messages.dropped_count`) and the item is repaired or dropped
like any other failed check.
- [ ] Unit tests with fixture texts that match, mismatch and name nothing.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/ai/src/validator/`, `backend/crates/ai/src/output/{report,weekly}.rs`,
`backend/crates/ai/src/plan/`. Spec section 2 (the language layer).

title: Why this? data for every recommendation
body: ## Problem
A player told "work on missed mates first" cannot see why: which counts, which comparison, which rule.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One server function per recommendation kind (top weakness, weekly focus and target, drill, plan
item) returns its facts: events and chances, the rate with its 80% range, the comparison and its
group, the points lost per game, the ranking rule in words, and the `algorithm_id`.
- [ ] Read from the stamped rows only; no new computation in the web.
- [ ] Unit tests for each kind, including "not ranked: not enough evidence yet" (ADR 0101).
- [ ] The UI is v0.5's ("Why this? on every recommendation"); this issue ships the data and a test.
## Pointers
- `apps/web/src/server/profile`, `server/focus`, `server/train`. Spec section 9.

title: Run records: the algorithm, the machine and the seeds with every benchmark run
body: ## Problem
`bench-results.json` (`RunOutput`, `backend/crates/bench/src/run.rs`) holds the scorecard, the suite,
the searches, the cache hits and the seconds, but not the algorithm, the commit or the machine. Two
runs cannot be compared fairly.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The run writes a RunRecord: `algorithm_id` and the manifest, the commit and a clean-tree flag,
the suite, its seeds and data checksums, the machine (CPU model, cores, RAM, OS), the Stockfish
banner (`engine::version::stockfish_version`) and binary sha256, the engine count, and per-stage
durations.
- [ ] `bench/run-record.schema.json` and a test that validates a fixture record against it.
- [ ] Existing readers of `bench-results.json` (`--baseline`, the workflow summary) keep working.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/bench/src/{run,results}.rs`, `.github/workflows/bench.yml`. Spec section 5.

title: A bench-history branch and cli bench compare
body: ## Problem
Each benchmark run is an artifact that expires after 30 days. There is no history and no way to say
whether version B is better than version A.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The weekly run of `.github/workflows/bench.yml` and the release workflow commit the RunRecord to
the `bench-history` branch as `runs/<date>-<suite>-<algorithm_id>.json`, with `contents: write`
on that job only. The branch is outside the `main` ruleset.
- [ ] `cli bench compare A B` (files or ids on the branch) prints per KPI: A, B, the difference with a
bootstrap 80% interval over seeds and players, and better, worse or no clear difference.
- [ ] Exit code 2 on a clear regression in a guarded KPI (the interval wholly on the worse side).
- [ ] Tests on two fixture records with a known difference.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/bench/src/results.rs` (`regressions`), `profile_core::stats::rng` for the seeded
bootstrap. Spec section 6.

title: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
Tier 1 (ADR 0100) measures whether the recommendation finds an injected flaw, and nothing measures the
rest against a ground truth: not the motif tagger, not the tablebase judgements, not the language
layer, and not real players. The latest scorecard (`docs/benchmark.md`) has recall at 2 of 0.6 and
calibration of 0.6, with three gaps open:
- #11: W4.missed (missing a mate) is not ranked in 80 games, because its peer row is low-sample;
- #13: W1's 80% interval is pulled towards the opponents' rate, so coverage fell to 0.6;
- #14: early-trap blunders that hang a piece now rank as W1, so W7.traps drops out for
`bench-opening`.
## Who it's for
Players, who are told what to practise; contributors, who change detectors and rankings; and anyone
checking our claims.
## Goals
1. A ground-truth suite per layer: Lichess puzzle themes for the tagger, Syzygy for endings, the lila
accuracy cases for the formula, more injected flaws and players from 600 to 2000 for the profile
and ranking, anonymised Lichess players for predictive validity, and deterministic checks for the
language layer.
2. Quality KPIs with 80% intervals over seeds and players, guarded in CI.
3. #11, #13 and #14 measured, and fixed or explained, here.
## Non-goals
- An LLM judge as a gate. It may be reported, never enforced.
- Real chess.com players' games in any suite.
## Evidence
- The motif tags are named after Lichess's puzzle themes already (`MotifTag`,
`backend/crates/profile-core/src/types.rs`), so the puzzle database (CC0) is a ready ground truth.
- `backend/fixtures/accuracy/lila-examples.json` is tested but not reported.
- `reference_games` already stores anonymised Lichess games (`white_hash`, `black_hash`).
## Proposed design
The spec (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-24-factual-deterministic-evaluation-design.md`), section 5: six deterministic suites with pinned snapshots and checksums, a
RunRecord per run (v0.2), the regression gate on guarded KPIs, and `ALGO_VARIANT` to run two
versions side by side on the same games.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every sub-issue below is done.
- [ ] The motif tagger's precision and recall are published per motif.
- [ ] Tier 2 reports the rank correlation and the lift at rank 1 with 80% intervals.
- [ ] The language checks show the recommendation in the text equals the computed one on 100% of the
fixed set (a failure is a bug).
- [ ] #11, #13 and #14 each have a measured result in the scorecard and are closed or have a recorded
decision.
## Test plan
- Each suite runs on a tiny fixture in CI (the full sample weekly), with fixed seeds.
- `cli bench compare` on a deliberate ranking variant shows the expected delta.
## ADR
ADR 0104. A new ADR when a ground truth is chosen or rejected (for example the puzzle sample size).
## Risks and open questions
- Puzzle themes label the solution, not every motif in the position, so precision may undercount;
a manual sample checks disagreements first.
- Tier 2 measures prediction, not improvement; Tier 4 (ADR 0090) is the measure for that.
## Pointers
- `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-24-factual-deterministic-evaluation-design.md`; `docs/benchmark.md`; ADRs 0100, 0101, 0104, ADR-R2-3 (clean-room tagger: data only, never
`cook.py`)
- `backend/crates/bench`, `backend/crates/profile-core/src/motifs`, `backend/crates/lichess-db`

title: Motif tagger against Lichess puzzle themes: precision and recall per motif
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
The motif tagger (ADR-R2-3) is tested on hand-built lines only. Nobody knows how often it calls a fork
a fork.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A pinned snapshot of `lichess_db_puzzle.csv.zst` (CC0) by sha256; a seeded sample of about
2,000 puzzles per theme for the themes `MotifTag` shares, committed as a small CSV.
- [ ] For each puzzle: play the opponent's first move, run `tag_line` on the solution, and compare
with the themes. `matingNet` has no Lichess theme and is not scored.
- [ ] Precision and recall per motif, with 80% Wilson ranges, in the RunRecord and the scorecard.
- [ ] The suite runs in CI on a 50-puzzle fixture and in the weekly run on the full sample.
- [ ] Credit to Lichess in `docs/evaluation.md` and `NOTICE`; no code from `cook.py`.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/profile-core/src/motifs/{rules,tag_line}.rs`, `MotifTag` in `types.rs`.
- Spec section 5, suite 1.

title: Tablebase agreement on endings with 5 pieces or fewer
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
Endgame judgements and the W8 detectors are only as right as the evaluations behind them, and the
tablebase (exact for 5 pieces or fewer) is never used to check them.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every position with 5 pieces or fewer in the replay fixtures and the puzzle sample, probed in the
pinned 3-4-5 set (`backend/crates/lichess-db/data/syzygy-345.sha256`).
- [ ] The share whose stored win, draw or loss judgement equals the tablebase's WDL, with the
disagreements listed by FEN.
- [ ] W8 events checked against DTZ: a W8 event where the tablebase says the result did not change is
a false positive.
- [ ] Skips cleanly (and says so) without the tables outside Docker; fails under `IN_DOCKER=1`.
## Pointers
- ADR-R2-12 (local Syzygy probe), ADR-R2-22, `position_tb`, `enrich` (`tb_ms`, `tb_probes`).

title: Report the accuracy formula's difference from lila as a KPI
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
`backend/crates/chess-core/tests/game_accuracy.rs` checks the game-accuracy formula against
`backend/fixtures/accuracy/lila-examples.json`, but the result is pass or fail. A drift inside the
tolerance never shows.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The bench computes the largest absolute difference between `game_accuracy` and each case's
`lila` value, and writes it to the RunRecord and the scorecard.
- [ ] It is a guarded KPI: a clear increase fails the regression gate.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/chess-core/src/game_accuracy.rs`, ADR-FIX-C-1 (lila game accuracy).

title: More injected flaws: forks, pins, skewers, back rank, endgames, time, openings, tilt
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
Tier 1 injects five flaws (`hang`, `miss_mate`, `opening_blunder`, `low_clock_blunder`,
`no_convert`). W2, W3, W6, W7.prep, W8, W9a, W9c, W10 and W12 have no injector, so their detection
is unmeasured.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] New `bench::flaws` injectors: missed forks, pins and skewers (W3, by motif), a back-rank
weakness, endgame technique (W8, with the tablebase), getting short of time and rushing (W9a,
W9c), leaving the opening worse (W7.prep) and tilt after a loss (W12).
- [ ] A player with two or three flaws at once, scored on whether all of them reach the top 3.
- [ ] Each injector counts its key's chances the way the detector does, as the existing five do.
- [ ] The full suite's rate sweep covers each new flaw; the smoke suite gains one player per flaw only
if the run stays under 15 minutes.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/bench/src/flaws.rs`, `docs/benchmark.md` (the true rate), ADR 0100.

title: Synthetic players from 600 to 2000
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
Every Tier 1 player meets 16 opponents rated 1400 to 1600. The audience runs from about 600 to 2000, and
the peer benchmark, bands and Maia behave differently at the ends.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The suite generates players at 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, 1600, 1800 and 2000 with opponents in
the same band (`PEER_RATING_WINDOW` 150), and a clean control per band.
- [ ] The clean policy's loss cap scales with the band, set before the run and recorded in the suite.
- [ ] The scorecard reports recall and calibration per band.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/bench/src/{policy,suite,generate}.rs`, `profile/src/peer_benchmark.rs`,
`profile-core/src/bands.rs`.

title: Tier 2: does the top weakness predict where points are lost?
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
Tier 1 players are engines with injected flaws. Whether the top-ranked weakness of a real player
predicts where they lose points has never been measured.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A fixed, checksummed sample of anonymised players from one pinned Lichess month
(`reference_games`, hashed players), at least 200 players with 80 or more games each.
- [ ] Profile from games before a date T; points lost per key in the games after T.
- [ ] Spearman correlation between the ranking and the points lost after T, and the lift of the
top-ranked key over a baseline ranking by base rate, both with 80% bootstrap intervals.
- [ ] Runs weekly, not in CI; the sample's checksum is in the RunRecord.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/lichess-db` (`reference_select.rs`, `sample.rs`), ADR-R2-9, ADR 0100 (Tier 2).

title: Language-layer checks on a fixed set of coaching inputs (--live)
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
The validator's drop rate and citation coverage are visible only by reading the database, one report at
a time, and they are not tracked per prompt version.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `cli bench run --suite language --live` generates reports, chat answers and weekly reviews from a
fixed set of CoachingInputs (the Tier 1 players and
`backend/fixtures/coaching-input/valid-sample.json`).
- [ ] Deterministic scores: citation coverage, drop rate by reason, recommendation match (v0.2's check),
and forbidden claims, per prompt-set hash, with tokens and `cost_micro_usd` per item.
- [ ] Refuses to run when `CI` is set or without `--live`: it spends real tokens.
## Pointers
- `backend/crates/ai/src/validator/`, `backend/crates/ai/src/prompts.rs` (`prompt_set_hash`),
ADRs 0093 and 0102.

title: Fail a pull request on a clear regression in a guarded KPI, with ALGO_VARIANT
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
`.github/workflows/bench.yml` compares with fixed tolerances in `bench/baseline.json`. Tolerances

title: Epic: the scientific method for the algorithm
body: ## Problem
The algorithm's thresholds were chosen after their data was seen, and none has a sample-size
argument. `RANK_MIN_EXCESS_PER_GAME` (0.02, ADR 0101) was set after the first smoke run; the
benchmark's thresholds (recall at 2 of 0.8, coverage in [0.65, 0.95]) have no power analysis, and one
detection in the smoke suite moves recall by 20 points. #11 and #13 need statistics nobody has
written yet.
## Who it's for
Players, whose plan rests on these numbers; contributors, who change a detector or a prior and need
to show it helps; and anyone checking our claims.
## Goals
1. Every behaviour change (a threshold, the ranking, a detector, a prior) ships after a
pre-registered experiment, with its result published whatever it shows.
2. A Python lab in the repository that drives the real Rust algorithm, never a copy of it.
3. The first four experiments: the benchmark's size, the calibration of the 80% ranges, partial
pooling against the current priors, and a leakage-free Tier 2 design.
## Non-goals
- Python in the product's request path. The lab only analyses; changes are made in Rust.
- Pre-registration for refactors and copy changes; the replay goldens prove those (ADR 0104).
- PyO3 bindings, until the JSON bridge is too slow (a separate decision).
## Evidence
- `docs/benchmark.md`: five flawed players in the smoke suite, so one detection is 20 points of recall.
- ADR 0101's consequences: coverage fell from 0.8 to 0.6 when W1's interval was shrunk towards the
opponents' rate (#13), measured but not explained.
- K-Dense's Scientific Agent Skills give vetted local methods for power, design, Bayesian models and
review; nothing in them is chess-specific.
## Proposed design
ADR 0106. `cli lab analyse|profile|rank` is a versioned JSON bridge over the production code (schema
`lab-v1`); `lab/` is a uv-locked Python 3.12 image that calls it (`rematch_lab`); experiments live in
`lab/experiments/EXP-NNNN/` with a pre-registration from `docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`; CI reruns
each twice and compares `results.json` byte for byte; nine science skills are vendored and pinned.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every sub-issue below is done.
- [ ] EXP-0001 to EXP-0004 each have a decision in `lab/findings.md`, negative or not.
- [ ] Every behaviour change merged after this epic links its experiment.
## Test plan
- The bridge's golden files and the analyse round trip in the Rust gate; the pytest contract tests
and the experiment reruns in `.github/workflows/lab.yml`.
## ADR
ADR 0106. Each shipped change from an experiment gets its own ADR and algorithm version.
## Risks and open questions
- The JSON bridge starts one process per call; experiments with thousands of players may need
batching or bindings.
- Synthetic players are not human (ADR 0100); Tier 2 is where a finding meets real games.
## Pointers
- ADRs 0100, 0101, 0104 and 0106; `docs/evaluation.md` (How we do science on the algorithm);
`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`; `lab/`; `backend/crates/bench/src/lab.rs`; `.claude/skills/science/`

title: EXP-0001: size the benchmark with a power analysis
parent: Epic: the scientific method for the algorithm
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: the size of the smoke and full Tier 1 suites
(`backend/crates/bench/src/suite.rs`) and CI's tolerances in `bench/baseline.json`, which gate
every algorithm change.
- If the result is that some full suite within the 9,000-game weekly budget reaches 80% power for
+0.1 in recall at 2, we will resize to the cheapest such suite; if none does, we will resize to
the budget and register the change it can detect (the pre-registration's two branches).
- Expected cost: a pilot of 3,840 games, about 35 minutes with 4 engines at the documented 0.544
seconds a game, plus a power simulation of minutes; no AI tokens; about two days of maintainer
time.
- Value score: impact 2 × uncertainty 3 ÷ cost 1 = 6.
- Cheaper alternative? No closed form fits a paired rule on clustered data with unknown hit rates,
so a small pilot is the cheapest input; it is sized by compute, not "as big as possible".
## Problem
The smoke suite has five flawed players, so one detection is 20 points of recall at 2, and CI's
tolerances (0.2 for recall, 0.15 for coverage) were not derived from anything.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first.
- [ ] Pre-registered with the `statistical-power` skill: the players and games per flaw that give
80% power to detect a 0.1 change in recall at 2 (the primary), with the interval width coverage then reaches as a secondary,
clustered by player.
- [ ] The smoke and full suites resized from the result, and the CI tolerances in
`bench/baseline.json` set from it.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md`.
## Pointers
- `docs/benchmark.md`, `bench/baseline.json`, `backend/crates/bench/src/suite.rs`, ADR 0100

title: EXP-0002: are the 80% ranges calibrated?
parent: Epic: the scientific method for the algorithm
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: whether the 80% ranges every weakness shows need a fix to their prior or
weighting (`backend/crates/profile-core/src/stats/posterior.rs`, `n0`), the question of #13.
- If the result is that every primary coverage lies inside [0.75, 0.85], we will keep the ranges and
say they are calibrated on the registered grid; if any lies outside, we will register a comparison
experiment for a fix (EXP-0006).
- Expected cost: profile only, no engine: about 50,000 profile computations through `cli lab
profile`, under an hour in the lab image; no AI tokens; about two days of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 3 ÷ cost 1 = 9.
- Cheaper alternative? The smoke suite's 20 intervals already say 60%, but they mix detector error
with the interval's, so they cannot locate the fault; exact counts drawn from chosen rates are the
cheapest design that can.
## Problem
The target's 80% interval holds the true injected rate 60% of the time on the smoke suite (12 of
20), and W1's interval is pulled towards the opponents' rate (#13).
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first.
- [ ] Pre-registered: the coverage of the Beta-posterior and bootstrap intervals per weakness, sample
size and rating band, with a calibration curve; the player is the unit.
- [ ] Run through `rematch_lab` on the registered seeds; a fix is proposed only from this evidence.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md`, linked from #13.
## Pointers
- #13, `backend/crates/profile-core/src/stats/posterior.rs`, `docs/benchmark.md` (score b)

title: EXP-0003: partial pooling against the current priors
parent: Epic: the scientific method for the algorithm
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: the prior strengths `n0` (`backend/crates/profile-core/src/constants.rs`),
fixed constants today, against priors derived from partial pooling by band (#11).
- If the result is that pooling estimates rates clearly better (PSIS-LOO and coverage), we will port
new prior constants to Rust as a major algorithm version; if not, the constants stay and the
comparison is published.
- Expected cost: PyMC fits with 4 chains on Tier 1 and the Lichess reference sample, CPU-hours on
the lab image; no engine runs beyond the existing samples; no AI tokens; about three days of
maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 2 ÷ cost 2 = 3.
- Cheaper alternative? Partly: EXP-0006's lighter-prior candidates test the same lever on EXP-0002's
design at a fraction of the cost. If EXP-0006 settles `n0`, the kill rule closes this one.
## Problem
Each key's prior strength `n0` is a fixed constant (`profile-core/src/constants.rs`). Whether pooling
across players by rating band estimates rates better is untested, and W4.missed's thin peer row is
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first.
- [ ] Pre-registered with the `pymc` skill: a hierarchical model of weakness rates across players
(partial pooling by band) on Tier 1 and the Lichess reference sample, against the production

title: EXP-0004: pre-register a leakage-free Tier 2 design
parent: Epic: the scientific method for the algorithm
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: whether the ranking (`rank-v1`,
`backend/crates/profile-core/src/stats/priority.rs`) tells a real player where they lose points
next better than a ranking that knows nothing about them; with it the design Tier 2 implements
and the cohort EXP-0010, EXP-0011 and EXP-0012 reuse.
- If the result is that the key ranked first in month t takes a larger share of the player's points
lost in month t+1 than the base-rate ranking's first key, by the registered minimum lift with its
interval wholly above it, we will publish it as the recommendation's first evidence on real
players and run Tier 2 weekly on this design; if the interval lies wholly below the minimum, the
ranking becomes the next challenger's target (EXP-0010 first) and the site says plainly that the
top weakness does not yet predict better than the band's base rates.
- Expected cost: two stages. The design (a power simulation of the registered rule and the leakage
review): CPU minutes, about two days of maintainer time. The run: about 200 anonymised Lichess
players with 40 or more rated games in month t and 20 in month t+1, one time class, about 12,000
games through the production analysis, about 100 core-hours at 300,000 nodes (a third of that if
EXP-0008 allows 100,000); two monthly dumps streamed once each, with the hash-keyed selection
EXP-0009 also needs; no AI tokens; about three days of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 3 ÷ cost 2 = 4.5
- Cheaper alternative? None that decides. Tier 1 cannot: its players are engines with flaws we
injected, so the ranking is scored on what we put there. Lichess's own `[%eval]` comments would
save the engine time, but only for games whose players asked for analysis, a selected sample, and
not with the production facts. The owner's chess.com account is one player, one unit, and is not
in the cohort. The design stage is the cheap part and comes first: checking for leakage after
Tier 2 is built is what costs more.
## Problem
Whether a weakness Rematch flags for a real player in one month predicts the points that player
loses to it in the next has never been measured. Tier 1's players are synthetic, and a Tier 2 built
without a registered design can leak the future into the past through its features, its folds or
its split date.
- Layer: recommendation.
- Ground truth and data: points lost per weakness key in month t+1, from the production analysis of
anonymised players in the Lichess monthly database (many thanks to Lichess and its players),
followed from month t to t+1 by the pseudonym `sha256(salt ‖ lower(name))` with the same `--salt`
(`backend/crates/lichess-db/src/reference_select.rs`). The cohort is built in the lab's own
database: no chess.com account, and no account linked in the app, is in it.
- Runs: the design now; the run after EXP-0008 sets the node count.
- Primary metric: the lift at rank 1: the share of a player's month-t+1 points lost (over the
rankable keys) that falls on their month-t first key, minus the same share for the base-rate
ranking's first key, the player as the unit, with a seeded bootstrap over players.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first.
- [ ] Pre-registered with the `statsmodels` and `scikit-learn` skills: a chronological split per
player (the profile from month t only), player-grouped folds, a mixed-effects model of future
points lost by weakness rank, and the lift over a base-rate ranking.
- [ ] No month-t+1 game reaches the profile, the peer benchmark or the band reference the month-t
ranking uses; the critic's review checks it before the run.
- [ ] The lift over the player's own raw points lost per key in month t is a confirmatory secondary:
the shrinkage and the peer comparison earn their place only by beating it.
- [ ] The design is what the Tier 2 sub-issue of the evaluation lab implements.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md` and the experiment's `summary.md`.
## Pointers
- "Tier 2: does the top weakness predict where points are lost?" (this milestone),
`reference_games`, ADR 0100, ADR-R2-11 (the privacy rules), EXP-0009 (the same selection)

title: EXP-0005: measure the churn between two algorithm versions
parent: Epic: the scientific method for the algorithm
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: the size of the full and smoke suites, which EXP-0001 set under an assumed
churn of 0.10 (`backend/crates/bench/src/suite.rs`, `bench/baseline.json`).
- If the result is a churn whose interval lies below 0.10, we will re-size to the smaller suite it
allows (or keep the size and register the smaller change it then detects); if it lies above, we
will re-register the weekly suite's detectable change as larger than 0.15; if it straddles 0.10,
the suites stay.
- Expected cost: the candidate only, on EXP-0001's 32 pilot players (3,840 games), about 25 minutes
with 8 engines at EXP-0001's measured 0.39 seconds a game; the reference side is EXP-0001's run,
reused; no AI tokens; about a day of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 2 × uncertainty 3 ÷ cost 1 = 6.
- Cheaper alternative? This is the cheap form: it reuses EXP-0001's pilot players, its reference run
and the cached evaluations. It waits for a real candidate (EXP-0006's), and the kill rule closes
it if none comes.
## Problem
EXP-0001 sized the benchmark under an assumed churn (the share of reference hits a candidate
loses while it gains elsewhere) of 0.10. Nothing measured it, and it moves the players needed
for +0.1 in recall at 2 from 14 to 40 a flaw at 80 games (`lab/experiments/EXP-0001/decision.md`).
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first.
- [ ] Pre-registered with its own analysis (the churn is a constant in EXP-0001's frozen one): run
the reference and the first real candidate (EXP-0006's branch) on EXP-0001's registered pilot
players, and count per flaw the reference hits the candidate loses and the misses it gains,
with the player as the unit and an interval on the churn.
- [ ] The suites re-sized at the measured churn in either direction, with the caveat that one
candidate's churn estimates one kind of change; a decision in `lab/findings.md`.
## Pointers
- `lab/experiments/EXP-0001/`, `backend/crates/bench/src/suite.rs`, `bench/baseline.json`, #91

title: Choose the weekly benchmark budget for a 0.1 change in recall at 2
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
EXP-0001 found that the weekly full suite (8,960 games, 22 players a flaw) detects a change of 0.15
in recall at 2 80% of the time, not the 0.1 the spec asks for. Detecting 0.1 needs about 16,000

(`lab/experiments/EXP-0001/decision.md`, Next 2). This is a budget choice, not an experiment.
## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The choice is an ADR; `backend/crates/bench/src/suite.rs`, `bench.yml` and `docs/benchmark.md`
follow it, and EXP-0005 sizes the suite at the measured churn on top of it.

title: lab-v2: the lab calls the trajectory, change-state, weekly target and trainer rules
parent: Epic: the evaluation lab: every layer against its ground truth
body: ## Problem
Four experiments wait on rules the lab cannot call. `cli lab` has `analyse`, `profile`, `rank` and
`tag-motifs` (lab-v1), and ADR 0104 allows one implementation of each rule, so the lab may not
write its own in Python.
- EXP-0015 (value 9): the trajectory verdict, `backend/crates/profile/src/coaching/trajectory.rs`.
- EXP-0014 (value 6): the change states, `backend/crates/profile-core/src/timeline/`.
- EXP-0011 (value 6): the weekly target, `chooseTarget` and `focusProgress` in
`apps/web/src/server/focus/goal.ts`.
- EXP-0012 (value 4): the trainer's sources, `SOURCES` and `primarySource` in
`apps/web/src/server/train/model.ts`.
EXP-0010 needs none of this: it runs on `cli lab rank` and Tier 2's cohort.
This is enabling work, not an experiment. The cheaper route keeps each rule where it is: the two
Rust rules become `cli lab` steps over the production functions, like `rank`; the two TypeScript
rules are called through Node, from the same modules the app imports. Porting `goal.ts` or the
trainer to Rust for the lab would leave two implementations, or move the app's code for a reason
no experiment has asked for. Both files are already digested in `algorithm/manifest.json`, so a
change to them is an algorithm version (ADR 0105).
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `cli lab trajectory` and `cli lab timeline`: JSON on stdin and stdout, `schema_version` and
`algorithm_id` in every response, the schema in `lab/schemas/`, golden files in
`backend/crates/cli/tests/lab.rs`.
- [ ] A Node entry point in `apps/web` (`lab` steps `focus-target`, `focus-progress` and
`trainer-sources`) that calls the exported functions of `goal.ts` and `model.ts` and nothing
else, with the same envelope and `algorithm_id`; a Vitest golden test per step.
- [ ] `rematch_lab.trajectory`, `.timeline`, `.focus` and `.trainer`, with pydantic models checked
against the schema, and the lab image able to run the Node step.
- [ ] A test fails when the lab's Python computes a rule's result itself instead of calling the
step.
- [ ] EXP-0011, EXP-0012, EXP-0014 and EXP-0015 name the step they call in their registration.
## Pointers

rematch_lab", `backend/crates/bench/src/lab.rs`, `backend/crates/cli/src/lab_cmd.rs`,
`lab/rematch_lab/bridge.py`

title: EXP-0006: fix the prior and the weighting of the 80% ranges
parent: Epic: the scientific method for the algorithm
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: the prior strengths `n0` and the recency weighting behind every 80% range
(`backend/crates/profile-core/src/constants.rs`, `stats/posterior.rs`, `stats/weights.rs`), which
EXP-0002 found miscalibrated.
- If the result is a candidate whose worst coverage improves wholly on the better side with the
guards held, we will ship it as a major algorithm version; if not, the ranges stay and we will say
on the site, from EXP-0002, where they run narrow.
- Expected cost: the development and confirmatory runs of EXP-0002's design, profile only, about
half an hour on one core each at EXP-0002's measured 1,592 seconds; the guards add one full Tier 1
suite for the candidate (8,960 games, about an hour with 8 engines), with the reference's weekly
run reused; no AI tokens; about four days of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 3 ÷ cost 2 = 4.5.
- Cheaper alternative? It already reuses EXP-0002's generator and the weekly reference run. A
closed-form fix without the comparison would skip the guard on clean false alarms, which a lighter
prior can raise.
## Problem
EXP-0002 found the 80% ranges are not calibrated for players well above their peers' rate: 12
of 20 weakness x sample-size coverages lie outside [0.75, 0.85], down to 0.10 for W4.missed at 30
games; the low ones miss on the high side (the prior pulls towards the peers), and W5 at 250
games is too high. The recency weighting widens intervals (it treats weighted counts as real
ones) and discounts the data but not the prior. W1's under-coverage in the benchmark (#13) is
reproduced with exact counts: 0.53 at 30 games.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first.
- [ ] A candidate developed on development seeds of EXP-0002's design (`--seed-namespace
EXP-0006-dev`), disjoint from the confirmatory ones, among: a lighter prior for every key, a
prior that decays with the data's recency weights, and an interval on the weighted counts'
effective sample size (`(sum w)^2 / sum w^2`). The chosen candidate is frozen on its branch.
- [ ] Pre-registered comparison on fresh confirmatory seeds: primary, the worst of the 20
coverages; guarded, the coverage at the peers' rate, and Tier 1 recall at 2 and clean false
alarms on the full suite (a lighter prior can rank more noise).
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md`, linked from #13; a shipped change is a major algorithm
version with its CHANGELOG entry citing EXP-0006.
## Pointers
- #13, #92, `lab/experiments/EXP-0002/decision.md`, `backend/crates/profile-core/src/constants.rs`
(`n0`), `stats/priority.rs`, `stats/posterior.rs`, `stats/weights.rs`. The KPI snapshots'
bootstrap intervals need a `lab-v2` step before they can be measured the same way.

title: Confirm a champion swap on fresh seeds at release (ADR 0109)
parent: Epic: the scientific method for the algorithm
body: ## Problem
The arena reuses each live experiment's registered seeds for every version, and ADR 0109 names the
cost itself: a challenger can be tuned to them. Developing on other seed namespaces keeps an author
honest by convention only. A fixed held-out set would be tuned to in its turn once its results
were seen, so the release uses seeds nobody can know in advance: a namespace derived from the
release commit.
This is a protocol change, not an experiment. Each live experiment's registered design already
sets its power, so a replication at the registered size needs no sizing study: whatever such a
study found, we would replicate at the registered size.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] An amendment of ADR 0109: when a release's challenger is better than the champion on a
primary, `release.yml` runs that experiment's frozen `analysis.py` for both on the seed
namespace `holdout-<release commit sha>`, unknown until the commit exists and new for every
release.
- [ ] The swap waits for the replication, and fails it when the fresh-seed verdict on the primary is
worse, or a reject by the experiment's own rule; no clear difference passes, since the
replication has the registered power and no more.
- [ ] Only experiments whose primary moved replicate, so a release costs at most the seeded runs
once more: 2.9 CPU-hours today (EXP-0001 2.44, EXP-0002 0.44), inside the release budget of 8.
- [ ] An experiment whose frozen `analysis.py` cannot take a seed namespace is listed, and
replicates from its next registration on. One whose input is a fixed snapshot rather than
seeds holds out a share of it by hash: EXP-0020 and EXP-0021, which change the tagger, register
theirs from EXP-0007's puzzles.
- [ ] The fresh-seed records go to `lab/leaderboard.json` marked `holdout`, and the Experiments page
shows them beside the registered-seed records.
- [ ] An arena test: a planted challenger that wins on the registered seeds and loses on fresh ones
is held back.
## Pointers
- ADR 0109 (its consequences), `lab/rematch_lab/arena.py`, `.github/workflows/release.yml`,
`docs/evaluation.md` (the loop). `arena.py` and `lab/leaderboard.json` are maintainer-owned
sensitive paths (ADR 0108).

title: Epic: are the facts right?
body: ## Problem
Every recommendation rests on facts nobody has measured against an outside truth: the motif tags are
checked on hand-built lines only, and the 300,000-node search (`ENGINE_NODES`,
`backend/crates/engine/src/types.rs`) was chosen, not measured. If a fork is called a fork half the
time, or a blunder at 300,000 nodes is no blunder at 30 million, every layer above inherits the
error.
Every experiment here opens with a value case (the decision it informs, what each result would make
us do, the expected cost, the value score and the cheaper alternative), and it runs only while that
decision is open (the kill rule, `docs/evaluation.md`).
## Who it's for
Players, whose weaknesses are built from these facts; contributors, who change the tagger or the
engine settings; and EXP-0009, whose node count and motif keys come from here.
## Goals
1. EXP-0007: the motif tagger's precision and recall per tag against the Lichess puzzle themes, and
a rule for which tags we may name.
2. EXP-0008: whether 300,000 nodes is enough, on the cost and accuracy curve against a deep
reference, with Lichess's own evaluations as a second opinion on the judgements.
## Non-goals
- Building the suites themselves: the harnesses are the evaluation lab's sub-issues ("Motif tagger
against Lichess puzzle themes", "Tablebase agreement on endings with 5 pieces or fewer", "Report
the accuracy formula's difference from lila as a KPI").
- An experiment on the Syzygy agreement or the accuracy formula. Both are measured by those
sub-issues, and a disagreement there is a bug to fix, not a decision under uncertainty, so an
experiment would end in the same action either way.
## Evidence
- `MotifTag` (`backend/crates/profile-core/src/types.rs`) is named after the puzzle themes, so the
Lichess puzzle database (CC0) is a ready ground truth.
- The judgement rule (`backend/crates/chess-core/src/judgement.rs`: a fall in winning chances of
0.3, 0.2 or 0.1) is lila's published rule, so a disagreement with Lichess on the same move comes
from the evaluations, not the rule.
- The Lichess monthly database carries `[%eval]` comments on analysed games, and `lichess-db`
already detects them (`headers.rs`, `has_eval`).
## Proposed design
EXP-0007 runs first: it needs no engine. EXP-0008 follows, and its result sets the node count of
EXP-0009's cohort, the largest compute bill in the catalogue. Both run through `rematch_lab` on
pinned, checksummed inputs (ADR 0106).
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every sub-issue below is decided or closed under the kill rule, with its line in
`lab/findings.md`.
- [ ] The per-tag precision and recall, and the node-count curve, are published on the site's
Experiments page.
## Test plan
- Each experiment's `analysis.py` reruns twice in `.github/workflows/lab.yml` and gives
byte-identical `results.json`.
## ADR
ADR 0106 for the method. A shipped change (a withdrawn tag, a new node count) is a major algorithm
version with its own ADR.
## Risks and open questions
- Puzzle themes label the solution, not every motif in the position, so precision may undercount;
disagreements are checked by hand on a sample first.
- A 30-million-node search is a proxy for the truth, not the truth; the Syzygy tables are exact only
for 5 pieces or fewer.
## Pointers
- `docs/evaluation.md` (The experiment catalogue), ADRs 0104 and 0106, ADR-R2-3 (the clean-room
tagger), `backend/crates/profile-core/src/motifs/`, `backend/crates/engine/src/types.rs`

title: Epic: do we recommend the right thing?
body: ## Problem
Rematch tells a player what to practise, and nothing yet shows that what it picks is what helps
people improve. The teaching order comes from the research notes (`trainability`,
`backend/crates/profile-core/src/constants.rs`), the ranking from ADR 0101's choice of points lost
per game, the weekly target from a rule of thumb (ADR 0091: a quarter fewer), and the drills from
the player's own mistakes (ADR 0090). Each is a reasonable guess; none is checked against real
players.
Every experiment here opens with a value case (the decision it informs, what each result would make
us do, the expected cost, the value score and the cheaper alternative), and it runs only while that
decision is open (the kill rule, `docs/evaluation.md`).
## Who it's for
Every player, since this is the advice itself; and the maintainer, who has to decide what to teach
first.
## Goals
1. EXP-0009, the top priority: across real anonymised Lichess players, among those whose rating
rose, which weakness rates fell first and most. It tells us what to teach from data.
2. EXP-0010: ranking by points lost per game against ranking by frequency, on Tier 2's held-out
games (it builds on EXP-0004, #94).
3. EXP-0011: whether the weekly focus target is met by chance, or out of reach, for real players in
that band.
4. EXP-0012: whether drilled positions resemble the player's next mistakes.
## Non-goals
- Causal claims. EXP-0009 is observational: it names candidates to teach, and the learning
experiments (v0.6) test whether teaching them works.
- Real chess.com players' games. Every cohort is anonymised Lichess data.
## Evidence
- `reference_games` stores anonymised Lichess games with pseudonymous player hashes (`sha256(salt ‖
lower(name))`, `backend/crates/lichess-db/src/reference_select.rs`), and a build's salt can be
passed again with `--salt`, so the same players can be followed from month to month.
- The ranking's floor (`RANK_MIN_EXCESS_PER_GAME`, 0.02) was set after the first smoke run (ADR
0101), with no predictive check.
## Proposed design
EXP-0009 runs after the facts epic (its node count from EXP-0008, its motif keys from EXP-0007). It
is staged: a pilot on games that already carry Lichess's `[%eval]` comments (no engine time) sizes
the main cohort before any engine runs. EXP-0010, EXP-0011 and EXP-0012 reuse Tier 2's cohort and
profiles, so they cost minutes, not days.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every sub-issue below is decided or closed under the kill rule, with its line in
`lab/findings.md`.
- [ ] EXP-0009's result, whatever it shows, is on the site with its caveats about confounding, and
the trainability rows either cite it or say that it found no signal.
## Test plan
- Each experiment's `analysis.py` reruns twice in `.github/workflows/lab.yml`; the cohorts are
pinned by checksum in `inputs.sha256`.
## ADR
ADR 0106 for the method; a new ADR for the longitudinal cohort selection (a privacy-relevant change
to ADR-R2-11's selection), and one for each shipped change.
## Risks and open questions
- Regression to the mean, rating catch-up of new accounts and reverse causation can each make a
weakness look like the cause of a climb; EXP-0009 registers how it separates them, and what it
cannot separate it says.
- Following pseudonyms across months makes the data more identifying; the cohort keeps the hashes
only, and ADR-R2-11's rules apply.
- The target rule (ADR 0091) and the trainer (ADR 0090) are TypeScript, which the lab's bridge does
not call yet.
## Pointers
- ADRs 0090, 0091, 0101, 0106, ADR-R2-9 and ADR-R2-11; #94 (EXP-0004); the sub-issue "Tier 2: does
the top weakness predict where points are lost?"; `docs/research/improvement-engine.md`

title: Epic: is the profile right?
body: ## Problem
The profile says how often a player makes each mistake, when a weakness changed, and whether their
rating is clearly worse than at its peak. Its ranges are miscalibrated for players well above their
peers (EXP-0002, #92), and its thresholds and detectors were never tested for false alarms:
`min_evidence` (`backend/crates/profile-core/src/constants.rs`), the timeline detectors
(`backend/crates/profile-core/src/timeline/`) and the trajectory verdict (ADR 0089).
Every experiment here opens with a value case (the decision it informs, what each result would make
us do, the expected cost, the value score and the cheaper alternative), and it runs only while that
decision is open (the kill rule, `docs/evaluation.md`).
## Who it's for
Every player, from the first 30 games on; and contributors who change a threshold or a detector.
## Goals
1. EXP-0013: how often a player with no weakness is shown one, by games played.
2. EXP-0014: how fast the change detectors confirm an injected improvement or regression, and how
often they raise a false one.
3. EXP-0015: how often the trajectory says "clearly worse" for a player whose strength did not
change.
4. Linked, not repeated: EXP-0002 (calibration of the 80% ranges, #92), EXP-0003 (partial pooling,
#93), and EXP-0006 (the fix EXP-0002 calls for), all under "Epic: the scientific method for the
algorithm".
## Non-goals
- Real players' games: every experiment here uses synthetic series whose truth we set, so none needs
an engine run.
## Evidence
- EXP-0002's design (event counts drawn from chosen rates, fed to the production estimate) runs
without an engine; EXP-0013 reuses it at the peers' rate.
- ADR 0089's "then" window is centred on the rating peak, a selected maximum, so a player whose
rating only wanders may often be told "worse".
## Proposed design
All three are simulations through `rematch_lab`. EXP-0013 uses `cli lab profile` and `cli lab rank`
as they are (lab-v1); EXP-0014 and EXP-0015 need a `cli lab timeline` and a `cli lab trajectory`
step (lab-v2) over the production Rust code. They need no engine, so they can run alongside the
facts epic.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every sub-issue below is decided or closed under the kill rule, with its line in
`lab/findings.md`.
- [ ] The false-alarm rates and the detection curve are published beside the features they describe.
## Test plan
- Each experiment reruns twice in `.github/workflows/lab.yml`; the lab-v2 steps get golden files in
`backend/crates/cli/tests/lab.rs`.
## ADR
ADR 0106; a lab-v2 schema change gets a note in its ADR's consequences; a shipped change is a major
algorithm version with its own ADR.
## Risks and open questions
- Synthetic series are not human (ADR 0100): the noise model of each is registered and varied in a
sensitivity analysis.
## Pointers
- #92, #93, ADRs 0089, 0101, 0106; `backend/crates/profile-core/src/constants.rs`,
`stats/priority.rs`, `timeline/`; `backend/crates/profile/src/coaching/trajectory.rs`

title: Epic: is the AI faithful?
body: ## Problem
The coach writes citation tokens, the server fills in the numbers, and the validator
(`backend/crates/ai/src/validator/`) drops anything uncited. Nobody has measured what the validator
misses when a text is wrong on purpose.
Every experiment here opens with a value case (the decision it informs, what each result would make
us do, the expected cost, the value score and the cheaper alternative), and it runs only while that
decision is open (the kill rule, `docs/evaluation.md`).
## Who it's for
The friends in the beta, who will read the coach's words; and contributors who change a prompt or a
validator rule.
## Goals
1. EXP-0016: the validator's catch rate on planted faults, then, with `--live`, how often the model
writes such text from adversarial coaching inputs.
## Non-goals
- An experiment on recommendation fidelity. Whether the text names the computed recommendation is a
deterministic check with a 100% target (v0.2's "Check that the recommendation a text names is the
computed one"); a failure is a bug, so both results lead to the same action.
- An experiment on the drop rate and tone per prompt version. The lab sub-issue "Language-layer
checks on a fixed set of coaching inputs (--live)" tracks the drop rate per prompt-set hash; a
comparison becomes an experiment only when a prompt change is proposed. Tone is judged by an LLM
at best, and an LLM judge never gates (`docs/evaluation.md`).
- Spending tokens in CI. `--live` runs only by hand.
## Evidence
- The validator has rules for evidence, bounds, focus, format, language and leaks
(`backend/crates/ai/src/validator/`), and `backend/fixtures/coaching-input/valid-sample.json` is a
fixed input to mutate.
## Proposed design
EXP-0016 is staged: a deterministic mutation set first (no tokens), and the `--live` stage only if
the first passes, so no tokens are spent on a validator already known to leak.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every sub-issue below is decided or closed under the kill rule, with its line in
`lab/findings.md`.
- [ ] The catch rate per fault class is published on the site.
## Test plan
- Stage 1 reruns twice in `.github/workflows/lab.yml`; stage 2 refuses to run when `CI` is set or
without `--live`.
## ADR
ADR 0106; a new validator rule from this is a minor algorithm version (ADR 0105).
## Risks and open questions
- Planted faults are the ones we thought of; the `--live` stage is there to find the ones we did
not.
## Pointers
- ADRs 0093, 0102, 0104, 0106; `backend/crates/ai/src/validator/`,
`backend/crates/ai/src/prompts.rs` (`prompt_set_hash`)

title: EXP-0007: the motif tagger against the Lichess puzzle themes
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: which motif tags Rematch may name to a player. The tags name the missed-motif
series (`motif.missed:<tag>`, `backend/crates/profile/src/timeline_job.rs`), the motif of a
drilled position after the attempt (`move_features.best_line.tags`, ADR 0090), and the coach's
evidence.
- If the result is a tag whose precision lies below the registered floor, we will stop naming that
tag to players (it is still computed) until a fixed rule passes the same suite; if every tag
clears the floor, we will keep them all and publish precision and recall per tag as KPIs.
- Expected cost: no engine: `tag_line` replays each puzzle's own solution. About 30,000 puzzles
(2,000 for each of the 15 tags with a Lichess theme), CPU minutes on one core; no AI tokens; a
one-off download of the puzzle database; about two days of maintainer time on top of the harness
sub-issue.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 3 ÷ cost 1 = 9.
- Cheaper alternative? No. The unit tests' hand-built lines were written by the authors of the
rules, so they cannot measure them; the sample per theme is the power analysis's call, not a
cheaper study. It reuses the harness of "Motif tagger against Lichess puzzle themes".
## Problem
How often is a position Rematch calls a fork really a fork, and how many forks does it miss?
- Layer: facts.
- Ground truth and data: the themes of the Lichess puzzle database (CC0, many thanks to Lichess and
its players), from a snapshot pinned by sha256 and a seeded sample per theme. `mateIn4Plus` is
scored against `mateIn4` and `mateIn5`; `matingNet` has no theme and is not scored.
- Runs: now.
- Primary metric: precision per tag with Wilson intervals, Bonferroni-corrected over the 15 tags,
each against the registered floor; recall is a confirmatory secondary.
- Files and constants: `backend/crates/profile-core/src/motifs/rules.rs` (`SACRIFICE_PAWNS` 2),
`motifs/tag_line.rs` (`SETTLE_EXTRA` 4, `MAX_REPLAY_PLIES` 128), `MotifTag` in
`backend/crates/profile-core/src/types.rs`.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first, then the
rest of the template; the kill rule applies if the decision above closes first.
- [ ] The disagreements of a seeded sample are checked by hand before the run, since a theme labels
the solution and not every motif in the position; the share found to be label gaps is
registered as a correction or as a caveat, decided before the results.
- [ ] No code from Lichess's `cook.py` (ADR-R2-3): its data only.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md` whatever it shows, and the experiment's `summary.md`.
## Pointers
- "Motif tagger against Lichess puzzle themes" (the harness, this milestone), ADR-R2-3,
`docs/evaluation.md`

title: EXP-0008: is 300,000 nodes enough? Depth against judgements and cost
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: `ENGINE_NODES` (300,000, `backend/crates/engine/src/types.rs`, protocol
`sf19-n300k-v1`), the largest compute cost of the pipeline, and with it the node count of
EXP-0009's cohort.
- If the result is that 100,000 nodes agrees with the deep reference within the registered margin of
300,000's agreement, we will propose a 100,000-node protocol (a third of the engine time a game)
as a major algorithm version; if 300,000 nodes falls short of the reference by more than the
margin, we will propose a higher count and re-cost the pipeline; otherwise 300,000 stays and the
curve is published.
- Expected cost: 40 seeded games (about 4,000 positions) searched at 50,000, 100,000, 300,000, 1
million and 3 million nodes, and a 30-million-node reference: about 140 billion nodes, about 40
core-hours at an assumed 1 million nodes a second a thread (the pipeline benchmark measures the
real rate); no AI tokens; about two days of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 2 ÷ cost 2 = 3. It runs early despite the score because
EXP-0009's cost depends on it.
- Cheaper alternative? Partly. Lichess's own `[%eval]` comments in the monthly database cost no
engine time, but they come from another build and depth, so they show whether we agree with
Lichess, not whether 300,000 nodes is enough. They are this experiment's secondary, which replaces
a separate experiment on judgements against Lichess's (the judgement rule is lila's, so a
disagreement can only come from the evaluations). The 300,000-node evaluations are reused from
`position_evals`.
## Problem
Does a 300,000-node search give the same judgements (blunder, mistake, inaccuracy) and the same best
move as a search a hundred times deeper, and what does each step down or up cost?
- Layer: facts.
- Ground truth and data: a single-thread **Stockfish 19** search at 30 million nodes as the
reference (exact Syzygy results where 5 pieces or fewer remain); for the secondary, Lichess's
`[%eval]` comments on the same games from the monthly database.
- Runs: now.
- Primary metric: judgement agreement: the share of moves whose judgement at N nodes equals the
reference's (`backend/crates/chess-core/src/judgement.rs`: a fall in winning chances of 0.3, 0.2
or 0.1), with the game as the cluster, at each N; the decision reads 100,000 and 300,000.
- Files and constants: `ENGINE_NODES` and `ANALYSIS_PROTOCOL` in
`backend/crates/engine/src/types.rs`, `backend/crates/analysis/src/evaluate.rs`,
`backend/crates/chess-core/src/judgement.rs` and `score.rs` (`WIN_K`, `CP_LIMIT`), `engine_nodes`
in `backend/crates/algo/src/lib.rs`.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first, then the
rest of the template; the kill rule applies if the decision above closes first.
- [ ] Secondaries registered: best-move agreement, the absolute win% error, game accuracy, and
agreement with Lichess's judgements on games carrying `[%eval]`.
- [ ] The engine count, threads (1) and hash (16 MB) are held fixed; the reference's own settings
are registered.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md` whatever it shows, and the experiment's `summary.md`.
## Pointers
- ADR 0104 (determinism), ADR-R2-12 (Syzygy), `docs/benchmark.md`, the pipeline speed scorecard
(this milestone)

title: EXP-0019: a blind human audit of the motif tags the Lichess themes cannot judge
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: whether `hangingPiece`, `skewer`, `sacrifice` and `backRankMate`, hidden
by EXP-0007 pending an audit, are named to players again, fixed, or kept hidden.
- If the result is a tag whose audited precision is shown to be at least 0.80, we will name it
again; if it is shown below, its rule is fixed under its own experiment; otherwise it stays
hidden.
- Expected cost: a person judges a seeded sample of the puzzles we tag (the size from the power
analysis; EXP-0007's precisions suggest about 60 a tag, 240 positions), blind to our tags; about
a day and a half of maintainer time; no engine, no AI tokens.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 3 ÷ cost 2 = 4.5
- Cheaper alternative? No. The themes cannot tell our errors from their own gaps (EXP-0007's hand
check judged 19 of 26 checked false positives to be label gaps, but it was the agent's, unblind),
and the protocol keeps an LLM's judgement out of any decision (`docs/evaluation.md`).
## Problem
EXP-0007 measured precision against Lichess's generated themes at 0.57 (`hangingPiece`), 0.81 (`skewer`,
not shown to clear 0.80), 0.53 (`sacrifice`) and 0.61 (`backRankMate`), with recall of 0.82 to 1.00.
A recall near 1 with a low precision means our rule is wider than the theme, not necessarily wrong.
- Layer: facts.
- Ground truth and data: a person's verdict, blind to our tags, against the definition the product
intends, written down before the audit (with Lichess's published theme description beside it),
on a seeded sample of EXP-0007's confirmatory puzzles that we tag.
- Runs: now.
- Primary metric: audited precision per tag, with Bonferroni intervals over the four tags.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first, then the
rest of the template; the kill rule applies if the decision above closes first.
- [ ] The intended definition of each tag is written down before the audit, and where it differs
from Lichess's published theme, the difference is stated.
- [ ] No code from Lichess's `cook.py` (ADR-R2-3): its published descriptions only.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md` whatever it shows, and the experiment's `summary.md`.
## Pointers
- EXP-0007 (`lab/experiments/EXP-0007/decision.md`, `pilot/hand-check.md`), ADR-R2-3,
`backend/crates/profile-core/src/motifs/rules.rs`

title: EXP-0020: fix the deflection rule (attraction is not deflection)
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: the `deflection` rule (`backend/crates/profile-core/src/motifs/rules.rs`),
hidden by EXP-0007 (precision 0.56, recall 0.33 against the Lichess themes).
- If the result is a candidate rule whose precision is shown to be at least 0.80 on EXP-0007's
suite with recall not worse, we will ship it as a major algorithm version and name the tag
again; if not, the tag stays hidden.
- Expected cost: EXP-0007's suite reused (54,987 puzzles, CPU minutes, no engine); a candidate
developed on the pilot's 1,874; about two days of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 2 × uncertainty 2 ÷ cost 1 = 4
- Cheaper alternative? No. The suite, the sample and the analysis already exist; only the rule
changes.
## Problem
Our deflection fires on luring a piece to a square (16% of its false positives carry `attraction`,
13% `fork`), and misses a king driven off a square by check (EXP-0007's hand check, `4uKvP`) and a win
that comes two moves after the deflection (`eE9oz`). Of Lichess's deflection puzzles we tag 36%
`sacrifice` and 16% `pin`, and only 33% `deflection`.
- Layer: facts.
- Ground truth and data: EXP-0007's snapshot, sample and analysis, unchanged.
- Runs: now.
- Primary metric: the candidate's precision against the themes, against the floor of 0.80.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first, then the
rest of the template; the kill rule applies if the decision above closes first.
- [ ] A comparison against `algo-1.1.0+fa5e2186e1dd` on EXP-0007's confirmatory sample, the candidate
developed on the pilot only; recall and the other tags' precision are guarded.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md` whatever it shows, and the experiment's `summary.md`.
## Pointers
- EXP-0007 (`results.json`, `confusion`), `rules.rs` (`deflection`)

title: EXP-0021: fix the pin rule (recall 0.20)
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: the `pin` rule (`rules.rs`), hidden by EXP-0007. Its recall, 0.20 [0.18,
0.22] against the Lichess themes, needs a fix whatever an audit says about its precision (0.40).
- If the result is a candidate whose recall is shown to be at least 0.50 and precision not worse,
we will ship it as a major algorithm version; if not, the tag stays hidden.
- Expected cost: EXP-0007's suite reused, CPU minutes; about two days of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 2 × uncertainty 3 ÷ cost 1 = 6
- Cheaper alternative? No; the suite exists and only the rule changes.
## Problem
Our pin counts a pinned piece only when the swing's capture takes it inside the window. A pin that
stops a recapture (`5UyIN`, a smothered mate behind a pinned pawn) and a pinned piece taken after an
early gain (`auo2d`) are missed. 24% of the puzzles we tag `pin` carry Lichess's `deflection`, and 16%
of Lichess's deflection puzzles get our pin: the two rules fire on the same overloaded defenders.
- Layer: facts.
- Ground truth and data: EXP-0007's snapshot, sample and analysis, unchanged.
- Runs: now.
- Primary metric: the candidate's recall against the themes, against the floor of 0.50.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first, then the
rest of the template; the kill rule applies if the decision above closes first.
- [ ] A comparison against `algo-1.1.0+fa5e2186e1dd` on EXP-0007's confirmatory sample, the candidate
developed on the pilot only; precision and the deflection overlap are guarded.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md` whatever it shows, and the experiment's `summary.md`.
## Pointers
- EXP-0007 (`results.json`, `pilot/hand-check.md`), `rules.rs` (`pin`)

title: EXP-0022: motifs after the first gain and past ply 8
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: the window the motif rules read (plies up to the swing's depth plus one)
and `LINE_MAX_PLIES` 8 (`backend/crates/profile-core/src/features/derive.rs`).
- If the result is that a wider window raises recall with precision held, we will propose it as a
major algorithm version; if precision falls past the floor, the window stays and the recall loss
is published.
- Expected cost: EXP-0007's suite reused, re-scored by solution length and by the ply of the motif;
CPU minutes; about two days of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 2 ÷ cost 1 = 6
- Cheaper alternative? Partly: re-scoring EXP-0007's results by solution length shows where the
recall is lost before any rule changes, and runs first.
## Problem
In EXP-0007 recall falls with the puzzle's rating for every trusted motif: `fork` 0.86 (below 1000) to
0.61 (1700 to 1999) and 0.54 above 2000, `discoveredAttack` 0.95 to 0.71, `promotion` 0.83 to 0.70,
`sacrifice` 0.95 to 0.57. The hand check found the swing settling at the first gain, so a motif after
an early capture is outside the window, and lines that win only after ply 8 get no tag at all.
- Layer: facts.
- Ground truth and data: EXP-0007's snapshot, sample and analysis, unchanged.
- Runs: now.
- Primary metric: `fork` recall over the audience, the largest-volume motif.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first, then the
rest of the template; the kill rule applies if the decision above closes first.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md` whatever it shows, and the experiment's `summary.md`.
## Pointers
- EXP-0007 (`results.json`, `by_band`), `motifs/tag_line.rs`, `features/derive.rs`

title: EXP-0023: do the tags of the engine's best line match the tags of the puzzle's solution?
body: ## Value case
- Decision it informs: whether EXP-0007's precision and recall, measured on puzzle solutions, hold
for production, which tags **Stockfish 19**'s own best line at 300,000 nodes.
- If the result is that the tags agree on at least 90% of a seeded sub-sample, EXP-0007's KPIs are
published as production's; if not, the motif KPIs are re-measured on engine lines.
- Expected cost: about 300 audience puzzles of EXP-0007's sample, one 300,000-node search each (about
90 million nodes, minutes on one core); `cli lab tag-motifs` gains an engine option; about a day
of maintainer time.
- Value score: impact 3 × uncertainty 2 ÷ cost 2 = 3
- Cheaper alternative? No; nothing else compares the two lines.
## Problem
A puzzle's solution stops when the win is clear; the engine's best line goes on and may take another
order of moves. EXP-0007's claims are about solution lines only.
- Layer: facts.
- Ground truth and data: the tags of the solution line, against the tags of the engine's line, on
the same positions.
- Runs: now (one engine-heavy run at a time across lanes).
- Primary metric: the share of puzzles whose tag set is the same on both lines.
## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Pre-register before running (`docs/experiments/TEMPLATE.md`), the value case first, then the
rest of the template; the kill rule applies if the decision above closes first.
- [ ] The engine settings are production's (`sf19-n300k-v1`), through the Rust engine crate.
- [ ] A decision in `lab/findings.md` whatever it shows, and the experiment's `summary.md`.
## Pointers
- EXP-0007 (`preregistration.md`, section 2), `bench::lab::tag_motifs`
